title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
description:
Given an array nums, return the length of its longest strictly increasing subsequence. A subsequence keeps the original left-to-right order but may skip any number of elements between chosen values. It need not occupy consecutive positions. Strictly increasing means every selected value is greater than the previous selected value, so equal values cannot extend the length. Return a number rather than an actual subsequence.

One useful subproblem asks for the best increasing subsequence that ends at a particular position. It can extend an earlier ending only when that earlier value is smaller. Alternatively, track the smallest possible final value for each attainable subsequence length; a smaller tail is easier to extend later. Both views show why choosing the next biggest value greedily is unsafe: a big early pick can block many later picks.

An empty array has no subsequence of positive length and yields zero. One element always yields length one regardless of its value. Negative values and repetitions are allowed. For example, 10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18 contains an increasing subsequence 2, 3, 7, 18 of length four, although several other length-four answers exist; only the common length matters.

Example 1:

Input: nums = [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18]
Output: 4

Example 2:

Input: nums = [0,1,0,3,2,3]
Output: 4

Example 3:

Input: nums = []
Output: 0

Constraints:

  • 0 <= nums.length <= 2,500
  • -10,000 <= nums[i] <= 10,000
  • Selected indices must stay in increasing order.
